proposals.before: Qu Yuan followed Chu into exile and wrote his celebrated piece on the noble orange.
proposals.after: Qu Yuan was banished from Chu and wrote his celebrated piece on the noble orange.
proposals.reason: Chinese 逐楚 means he was driven out from Chu, not that he followed Chu into exile.

proposals.before: Lingjun followed Chu into exile and composed the chapter of auspicious calamity.
proposals.after: Lingjun was banished from Chu and composed the chapter of auspicious calamity.
proposals.reason: Same error as the idiomatic line: 逐楚 is banishment from Chu, not following Chu.

proposals.before: Under Emperor Xiaowen, literary culture flourished as never before: students were as numerous as ox hairs, but those who truly succeeded were as rare as unicorn horns. Confucius said, "Talent is hard to find—is that not exactly the case?"
proposals.after: Under Emperor Suzong, literary culture flourished as never before: students were as numerous as ox hairs, but those who truly succeeded were as rare as unicorn horns. Confucius said, "Talent is hard to find—is that not exactly the case?"
proposals.reason: Chinese 肅宗 is Emperor Suzong (Xiaoming), not Emperor Xiaowen (高祖).

proposals.before: Yuan Yue, whose style was Jingteng, came from Chen commandery and was the younger brother of Minister of Works Yuan Fan.
proposals.after: Yuan Yue, whose style was Jingteng, came from Chen commandery and was the younger brother of Minister Yuan Fan.
proposals.reason: Chinese 尚書 denotes the Masters of Writing / minister, not Minister of Works (司空).

proposals.before: Yuan Yue, style name Jingteng, was a man of Chen commandery and the younger brother of Minister of Works Yuan Fan.
proposals.after: Yuan Yue, style name Jingteng, was a man of Chen commandery and the younger brother of Minister Yuan Fan.
proposals.reason: Same 尚書 mistranslation as in the idiomatic field.

proposals.before: He was so submitted to by things.
proposals.after: Such was the deference things showed him.
proposals.reason: The literal English is ungrammatical and obscures 為物所伏.

proposals.before: After the campaign he was appointed director of central arms in the left secretariat of the Ministry of Works, and soon died.
proposals.after: After the campaign he was appointed director of central arms in the left secretariat of the Masters of Writing, and soon died.
proposals.reason: 尚書 denotes the Masters of Writing / Department of State Affairs, not the Ministry of Works (工部).

proposals.before: On return he was made Director of Central Arms in the Left Secretariat of the Ministry of Works and died.
proposals.after: On return he was made Director of Central Arms in the Left Secretariat of the Masters of Writing and died.
proposals.reason: 尚書 is not the Ministry of Works; render as Masters of Writing / Department of State Affairs.

proposals.before: Though the superior medicines of Lord Tong of the Divine Farmer sometimes helped;
proposals.after: Though Lord Tong's superior medicines sometimes took effect;
proposals.reason: Chinese has only 桐君上藥; 'of the Divine Farmer' is an invented gloss not present in the source.

proposals.before: Bomao was born after his brothers Gui and lived apart from his elder brother Jingrong.
proposals.after: Bomao had earlier been adopted as heir to his paternal uncle Zhonggui, and lived apart from his elder brother Jingrong.
proposals.reason: 出後其伯仲規 means he was adopted to continue the line of his paternal uncle Zhonggui, not that he was born after brothers named Gui.

proposals.before: Bomao was born after his elder and younger brother Gui and lived separately from his elder brother Jingrong.
proposals.after: Bomao was first adopted as heir to his paternal uncle Zhonggui and lived separately from his elder brother Jingrong.
proposals.reason: 先出後其伯仲規 is the adoption formula; 伯仲規 is uncle Zhonggui, not brothers Gui.

proposals.before: Shou was then at Jinyang and contributed his own piece on Bomao; its ten-character line read, "Facing the wind I think of Xu Xuan; over wine I think of Liu Gongrong."
proposals.after: Shou was then at Jinyang and contributed his own piece on Bomao; its ten-character line read, "Facing the wind I think of Xuandu; over wine I think of Gongrong."
proposals.reason: 玄度 is the courtesy name Xuandu (of Xu Xun), not the personal name 'Xu Xuan'; the couplet uses courtesy names 玄度 and 公榮.

proposals.before: When Xiao Baoyin opened a field headquarters as Cavalry General-in-Chief to campaign in Guanzhong, he appointed Ziming Eastern Pavillion Libationer and entrusted him with official correspondence.
proposals.after: When Xiao Baoyin opened a field headquarters as Cavalry General-in-Chief to campaign in Guanzhong, he appointed Ziming Eastern Pavilion Libationer and entrusted him with official correspondence.
proposals.reason: English misspells Pavilion as Pavillion in the office title Eastern Pavilion Libationer (東閤祭酒).

proposals.before: When Xiao Baoyin served as Cavalry General-in-Chief with an open headquarters to campaign against Guanzhong, he made Ziming Eastern Pavillion Libationer and entrusted him with literary documents.
proposals.after: When Xiao Baoyin served as Cavalry General-in-Chief with an open headquarters to campaign against Guanzhong, he made Ziming Eastern Pavilion Libationer and entrusted him with literary documents.
proposals.reason: Same Pavilion misspelling in the literal English office title.

proposals.before: His grandfather Gongzhi had served as a clerk in the household of Liu Yikang's Prince of Pengcheng; fleeing turmoil he returned to the north, and the family settled at Yuanqu in Jiyin, thus becoming natives of that district.
proposals.after: His grandfather Gongzhi had served as a clerk in the household of Liu Yilong's Prince of Pengcheng, Yikang; fleeing turmoil he returned to the north, and the family settled at Yuanqu in Jiyin, thus becoming natives of that district.
proposals.reason: Chinese 劉義隆彭城王義康 names Emperor Liu Yilong and then Prince of Pengcheng Yikang; the idiomatic English fuses them as "Liu Yikang's Prince".

proposals.before: His grandfather Gongzhi was a clerk in the household of Liu Yikang's Prince of Pengcheng; fleeing hardship he returned to the north, and the family settled in Yuanqu, Jiyin, thus becoming natives of that commandery and county.
proposals.after: His grandfather Gongzhi was a clerk in the household of Liu Yilong's Prince of Pengcheng, Yikang; fleeing hardship he returned to the north, and the family settled in Yuanqu, Jiyin, thus becoming natives of that commandery and county.
proposals.reason: Literal English repeats the same reversed/fused identification of 劉義隆 and 彭城王義康.

proposals.before: He was a lowly retainer of Prince Guangyang of Yuan Yuan; in the horse stables he taught the slave boys to write.
proposals.after: He was a lowly retainer of Prince Yuan of Guangyang; in the horse stables he taught the slave boys to write.
proposals.reason: 廣陽王淵 is Prince Yuan of Guangyang; 'Prince Guangyang of Yuan Yuan' garbles the title and doubles Yuan.

proposals.before: Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate Xu Hong received memorials from the four directions and answered swiftly; facing Yuan alone he pondered and said: "They have Gentleman Wen of the Secretariat there—his literary talent is formidable."
proposals.after: Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate Xu Hong received memorials from the four directions and answered swiftly; facing Yuan alone he pondered and said: "They have Gentleman Wen there—his literary talent is formidable."
proposals.reason: Chinese 溫郎中 has no Secretariat qualifier; the literal invents 'of the Secretariat'.

proposals.before: At the beginning of Jianyi, he was Southern Master of Guests Gentleman and compiled the Veritable Records.
proposals.after: At the beginning of Jianyi, he was Southern Master of Guests Gentleman and compiled the imperial diary.
proposals.reason: 起居注 is the court/imperial diary, not the Veritable Records (實錄).

proposals.before: Once he missed a day on duty; Prince Tianmu of Shangdang was then recording affairs of the Secretariat and was about to have him beaten; Zisheng fled.
proposals.after: Once he missed a day on duty; Prince Tianmu of Shangdang was then overseeing Secretariat affairs and was about to have him beaten; Zisheng fled.
proposals.reason: 錄尚書事 is the executive oversight post, not literal 'recording' of Secretariat affairs.

proposals.before: He replied, "The sovereign, because Tiger Cage was lost, has been reduced to this plight.
proposals.after: He replied, "The sovereign, because Hulao was lost, has been reduced to this plight.
proposals.reason: 虎牢 is the place-name Hulao, not a literal 'Tiger Cage'.

proposals.before: Editorial note 8 They urged Zisheng to help draft the presentation speech.
proposals.after: They urged Zisheng to help draft the presentation speech.
proposals.reason: Chinese 推子昇合陳辭 has no editorial-note rubric; the idiomatic English invents 'Editorial note 8'.

proposals.before: Editorial note 8 They pressed Zisheng to join in composing the formal address.
proposals.after: They pressed Zisheng to join in composing the formal address.
proposals.reason: Chinese 推子昇合陳辭 has no editorial-note rubric; the literal English invents 'Editorial note 8'.

proposals.before: "Qu Yuan followed Chu into exile and composed the chapter on 'auspicious calamity'"—Commentary: The phrase "Jia huo" (auspicious calamity) has no known source. The Songs of Chu, "Ode to the Orange" in the Nine Pieces, reads: "O sovereign's noble tree, the orange has come to take root here."
proposals.after: "Lingjun followed Chu into exile and composed the chapter on 'auspicious calamity'"—Commentary: The phrase "Jia huo" (auspicious calamity) has no known source. The Songs of Chu, "Ode to the Orange" in the Nine Pieces, reads: "O sovereign's noble tree, the orange has come to take root here."
proposals.reason: Chinese begins with 靈均; idiomatic substitutes Qu Yuan and should preserve the source style name Lingjun.

proposals.before: "In the third year of Yongxing"—Commentary: Yongxing was an era name of Tuoba Si (Emperor Daowu)
proposals.after: "In the third year of Yongxing"—Commentary: Yongxing was an era name of Tuoba Si (Emperor Mingyuan)
proposals.reason: Tuoba Si was Northern Wei Emperor Mingyuan; Emperor Daowu was Tuoba Gui. Yongxing (AD 409–413) belongs to Mingyuan, not Daowu.

proposals.before: A southern campaign against Jiang, Shu, and Chen Shuang's uprising—in the Comprehensive Records, volume 176, biography of Pei Bomao, "nan" (south) is written as "ji" (and).
proposals.after: A southern campaign against the Jiang-Shu rebel Chen Shuangchi—in the Comprehensive Records, volume 176, biography of Pei Bomao, "nan" (south) is written as "ji" (and).
proposals.reason: Chinese names the rebel 陳雙熾 (Chen Shuangchi); the English drops 熾 and splits Jiang and Shu as if separate from the personal name.

proposals.before: Southern campaign against Jiang and Shu, Chen Shuang's revolt—Comprehensive Records, scroll 176, Biography of Pei Bomao, reads "south" as "and".
proposals.after: Southern campaign against Jiang and Shu, Chen Shuangchi's revolt—Comprehensive Records, scroll 176, Biography of Pei Bomao, reads "south" as "and".
proposals.reason: Source personal name is 陳雙熾; English "Chen Shuang" omits the final character 熾.

proposals.before: Qu Yuan was banished from Chu and wrote his celebrated piece on the noble orange.
proposals.after: Qu Yuan was banished by Chu and wrote his celebrated piece on the noble orange.
proposals.reason: 逐 marks Chu as the authority that banished Qu Yuan; 'by Chu' avoids implying that he was expelled beyond Chu's borders.

proposals.before: Lingjun was banished from Chu and composed the chapter of auspicious calamity.
proposals.after: Lingjun was banished by Chu and composed the chapter of auspicious calamity.
proposals.reason: The literal should likewise identify Chu as the agent of Lingjun's banishment without adding a destination.

proposals.before: When Emperor Xiaozong held the throne, refinement flourished greatly; learners were like ox-hairs, achievers like unicorn horns. Confucius said, "Talent is hard to find—is it not so?"
proposals.after: When Emperor Suzong held the throne, refinement flourished greatly; learners were like ox-hairs, achievers like unicorn horns. Confucius said, "Talent is hard to find—is it not so?"
proposals.reason: 肅宗 is Emperor Suzong; the earlier review corrected the idiomatic line but missed the same erroneous name in the literal.

proposals.before: Yuan Yue, whose style was Jingteng, came from Chen commandery and was the younger brother of Minister Yuan Fan.
proposals.after: Yuan Yue, whose style was Jingteng, came from Chen commandery and was the younger brother of Yuan Fan, a Master of Writing.
proposals.reason: 尚書 is Yuan Fan's specific office, Master of Writing, rather than the generic title 'Minister.'

proposals.before: Yuan Yue, style name Jingteng, was a man of Chen commandery and the younger brother of Minister Yuan Fan.
proposals.after: Yuan Yue, style name Jingteng, was a man of Chen commandery and the younger brother of Yuan Fan, a Master of Writing.
proposals.reason: The literal should also preserve Yuan Fan's office as Master of Writing.

proposals.before: His grandfather Gongzhi had served as a clerk in the household of Liu Yilong's Prince of Pengcheng, Yikang; fleeing turmoil he returned to the north, and the family settled at Yuanqu in Jiyin, thus becoming natives of that district.
proposals.after: His grandfather Gongzhi had served under Liu Yilong as a Household Clerk to Liu Yikang, Prince of Pengcheng; fleeing turmoil, he returned to the north, and the family settled at Yuanqu in Jiyin, thus becoming natives of that district.
proposals.reason: 劉義隆 and 彭城王義康 are two people; this wording keeps Liu Yilong distinct from Liu Yikang and attaches the princely title to Yikang.

proposals.before: His grandfather Gongzhi was a clerk in the household of Liu Yilong's Prince of Pengcheng, Yikang; fleeing hardship he returned to the north, and the family settled in Yuanqu, Jiyin, thus becoming natives of that commandery and county.
proposals.after: His grandfather Gongzhi served under Liu Yilong as a Household Clerk to Liu Yikang, Prince of Pengcheng; fleeing hardship, he returned to the north, and the family settled in Yuanqu, Jiyin, thus becoming natives of that commandery and county.
proposals.reason: The literal should distinguish Liu Yilong from Liu Yikang and attach Prince of Pengcheng to Yikang.

decisions.reason: In the couplet 淳于出齊 / 靈均逐楚, 楚 is the place-complement parallel to 齊, so 'banished from Chu' is accurate; changing to agentive 'by Chu' is a stylistic reinterpretation, not a correction of error.
The same parallel 出齊 / 逐楚 supports place-of-origin 'from Chu' in the literal; 'by Chu' is not required by the Chinese and does not fix a mistranslation.
肅宗 is Emperor Suzong; the literal's 'Xiaozong' invents a different temple name and must be corrected to match the Chinese and the already-fixed idiomatic line.
尚書 is conventionally rendered 'Minister' (Shangshu) in this period; 'Master of Writing' is an alternative technical gloss, not a fix of a factual or semantic error in the original.
The literal's 'Minister Yuan Fan' already conveys 尚書翻 adequately; replacing it with 'Master of Writing' is a preferred office-title style, not a required correction.
The existing phrasing already names both 劉義隆 and 彭城王義康 and attaches the Pengcheng title to Yikang; the proposed rewrite is clearer but only stylistic, not a semantic repair.
